community.headline: Maldon Mud Race sponsor gives Basildon Hospital two Xbox gaming trolleys for young patients
community.summary: A £3,060 gift from JR Revell Ltd pays for portable consoles that can be wheeled to children's and teenagers' bedsides.
body: Basildon Hospital now has two portable Xbox gaming trolleys for children and teenagers, paid for by a £3,060 donation from JR Revell Ltd, main sponsor of the Maldon Mud Race. The trolleys can be wheeled to bedsides, so they also reach young patients too unwell to leave their rooms or who must isolate.

The firm chose Basildon because the partner of its operations manager, Ronnie Baker, works on two of the hospital's children's wards. This year's Mud Race raised more than £50,000 for local charities, and JR Revell entered its own team to add to the total.

One trolley will go in a new teen room being refurbished on the ward, and the other will move between the children's wards. Southend and Broomfield hospitals already have similar trolleys, which the trust says have proved popular.

community.headline: £25,000 gift transforms end-of-life rooms at Broomfield Hospital
community.summary: Friends at Broomfield Hospital, backed by Chelmsford Round Table, funded five refurbished rooms through the hospitals charity's Dandelion Appeal.
body: Five rooms on the care of the elderly and specialist stroke wards at Broomfield Hospital in Chelmsford have been made over for patients in their final days, thanks to a £25,000 donation. The money came from Friends at Broomfield Hospital, with support from Chelmsford Round Table, and was given to the Dandelion Appeal run by Mid and South Essex Hospitals Charity.

The side rooms are meant to feel more comfortable and homely, and give families a private space to be together. The appeal has also paid for overnight beds for relatives, recliner chairs and wall art. The Friends, who have supported the hospital for more than 75 years, were shown the finished project by end-of-life lead nurse Debbie Boulden.

Lucy Thomas-Clayton, the charity's director of charity and voluntary services, thanked the group, saying their support continues to make a lasting difference to patients and families. The Dandelion Appeal also funds end-of-life care improvements at Basildon and Southend hospitals.

community.headline: Volunteers wanted for Tesco winter food collection on 26 to 28 November
community.summary: Volunteers are sought for three-hour shifts at collection points in large Tesco stores, supporting Trussell food banks and the Felix charity network.

body: Foodbanks and food charities are looking for volunteers to stand at collection points in large Tesco stores for the supermarket's Winter Food Collection, which runs from 26 to 28 November. Volunteering takes about three hours, and the charities say having people in store significantly increases how much food is given.

This is the 14th year of the collection, run with charity partners Trussell and Felix, and last year shoppers donated almost 1.5 million meals' worth of food. One in five Trussell food parcels comes from Tesco and its customers, and more than half of the charities in the Felix network, which spans over 8,000 local groups, report rising demand over the past year.

People can sign up through the Trussell or Felix websites to help at their nearest large Tesco. Trussell's co-chief executive Matthew van Duyvenbode said volunteers were urgently needed to play their part.

body: Harlow charity Rainbow Services is holding a free Ageing Well drop-in next week aimed at reducing falls among older people in the town. The event runs from 10.30am to 1pm on Wednesday 11 November at GPCA in Abercrombie Way, and everyone is welcome without booking.

Its Community Builder team has organised the morning with Princess Alexandra Hospital and other local groups, with about 25 stalls offering advice on staying safe at home and on local support. Exhibitors include Essex Police, Peabody, Essex Wellbeing Service, Hearing Help Essex, Age Well East, Essex Libraries and Action for Family Carers, alongside talks and seated exercise sessions.

Free slippers with sturdy soles and supportive backs, funded by Chas Berger, will be handed out while stocks last. Organisers point out that one in three people over 65 fall each year, and Rainbow Services can be contacted on 07701 224342.

body: A former maths teacher at an Essex secondary school has been given a further prison sentence for sexual offences against girls, LBC reports. Syed Ahmed, 38, posed as a teenage boy on social media to contact girls aged 13 to 16.

Ahmed resigned after his arrest in May 2023. He was sentenced in September 2025 for offences including rape and meeting children after grooming, and at a second trial this year he admitted further online offences and was convicted of others he had denied. LBC and other outlets report he was jailed for a further 10 years at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday.
The school where he worked has not been named in the reports.

body: Scott Allaker, 50, of Beech Avenue, Brentwood, has pleaded guilty to five counts of shop theft committed between 8 August and 11 October.

Magistrates heard he took meat, wine, prosecco and champagne worth £1,117.55 in total from BP service stations including Herongate, the A13 at Orsett Cock and Hutton Mount, and from a Tesco in Brentwood. Roads policing officers stopped his car on London Road, Wickford, after a theft at the Hutton Mount site on 11 October and found eight bottles of champagne and one of prosecco.
He was given conditional bail barring him from BP, B&Q, Sainsbury's and Tesco stores in Essex and Suffolk, and is due to be sentenced on November 25.

courts.headline: Braintree driver banned after roof load smashed into armed police car on A120
courts.summary: A panel flew off his Audi near Stansted Airport, crossed the central barrier and shattered a police car's windscreen.
body: A Braintree driver whose unsecured roof load smashed into an Essex Police armed response car on the A120 near Stansted Airport has been banned from driving for a year. The panel flew off his Audi, cleared the central barrier and shattered the police car's windscreen, showering both officers with glass.

Glen Lillie, 34, of Park Drive, Braintree, pleaded guilty to three charges and was given a 12-month community order with 140 hours of unpaid work at Colchester Magistrates' Court on 22 October. The collision happened at about 1.30pm on 19 December 2025 near Little Canfield as officers drove to an emergency on blue lights. Lillie did not stop or report it, but police traced him through images of a car carrying a large flat item on a roof rack.

Police said the officer brought the damaged Volvo to a controlled stop, and the dual carriageway was closed while debris was cleared. The car was off the road for several months. PC Simon Bailey said the outcome could have been devastating and urged drivers to secure their loads.

official.headline: Essex PC dismissed after panel finds gross misconduct towards three female colleagues
official.summary: A misconduct hearing chaired by Assistant Chief Constable Glen Pavelin found PC Ben Norfolk's behaviour towards colleagues amounted to gross misconduct.
body: An Essex Police officer has been dismissed after a misconduct panel found he behaved in a coercive and controlling way towards female colleagues. PC Ben Norfolk was found to have committed gross misconduct at a hearing chaired by Assistant Chief Constable Glen Pavelin.

The allegations considered at the hearing related to his behaviour towards three colleagues between 2024 and 2025, and included sending intimate images of himself in uniform and suggesting sexual activity at work. Mr Pavelin called the conduct completely unacceptable and said it showed a complete disregard for the oath the officer took.
He said tackling violence against women and girls is a priority for the force, and thanked the colleagues who came forward for trusting the force to deal with it.

body: Essex Police's Rural Engagement Team has been awarded £57,721 from the Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner's Safer Streets fund to step up its fight against crime in the countryside. The money will be used across rural Essex, including the Dengie, where police have recently been cracking down on hare coursing.

The grant will buy a John Deere Gator all-terrain vehicle for remote locations, mobile number plate recognition cameras for three vehicles, trail cameras and signs for hotspots, and training for officers to drive the vehicle. Commissioner Roger Hirst said rural crime can have a significant impact on farmers, businesses and communities, and Supt Darren Deex said the funding would strengthen the team's response.

The commissioner's office says the kit will be sent wherever the data shows a rural crime hotspot, and is urging residents to report every crime so that resources can be targeted. Materials to support Farm Watch schemes are also included.

body: Colchester City Council's grounds maintenance service transferred to Amphora, the company the council wholly owns, on 1 November. The service looks after parks, sports grounds, open spaces, housing land, cemeteries and the crematorium across the city.

Around 40 former Idverde employees moved across, and council and Amphora staff marked the change with volunteering days at Castle Park on 2 and 3 November, clearing leaves and planting hundreds of spring bulbs. The service covers almost 13,000 assets over more than 870 hectares. Cllr Martin Goss, portfolio holder for waste, neighbourhoods and leisure, welcomed the new colleagues into the council family.
The council says the arrangement gives it more flexibility to respond to local priorities and to find new ways of improving parks and green spaces, while keeping investment in the local area.

official.headline: Great Baddow's Iron Age gold hoard goes into classrooms in new Museum of Chelmsford history kit
official.summary: Primary schools can now hire a hands-on box built around the 935 gold coins found in Great Baddow in 2020, designed with help from local pupils.
body: The Museum of Chelmsford has launched a hands-on history kit that lets primary pupils investigate one of the county's most striking finds, the Great Baddow Coin Hoard. The Baddow Discover Box is aimed at Key Stage Two classes and turns the 935 Iron Age gold coins found in Great Baddow in 2020 into a set of lessons on Chelmsford's prehistory.

The box holds 21 Iron Age activities, from handling replica artefacts to weighing up the evidence about who buried the hoard and why, and can be used as eight separate lessons or combined into an Iron Age Day. Pupils and teachers at Beehive Lane Community Primary School helped design and trial it with creative practitioner Hannelore Smith, and Westlands Community Primary and Moulsham Junior schools tested it in early 2026. It was funded by the National Lottery Heritage Fund through the Timeless Treasures project.

Schools can hire the box by the half term, with the next slot available from January 2027, and schools outside Chelmsford and Essex can borrow it too. Councillor Jennie Lardge, the city council's deputy leader, called it "all at once fun, inspiring and educational". Prices and other boxes, covering the Romans, Victorian toys and the Suffragettes, are listed on the museum's website.

Then manager Steve Tilson recalled that the players feared the worst when they saw the teamsheet. Southend went on to take Tottenham to extra time in the quarter-final before losing to a Jermain Defoe goal.

In current squad news, the club confirmed on Thursday that Sam Austin has joined Kidderminster Harriers on loan, and Kidderminster say the move runs until the end of the season. The jury convicted him over offences against four women at a London bar, at a radio studio, at his London home and on a Channel 4 project, all between 2004 and 2009. The Metropolitan Police said officers spoke to more than 100 witnesses and took over 400 statements during the investigation, which began after allegations were reported in September 2023.

stories.headline: Essex commissioner brands regional 'mega force' plan not fit for purpose as merger review awaits publication
stories.summary: Roger Hirst told the BBC there is no evidence bigger forces perform better, a day after the Met chief called for the 43 forces in England and Wales to shrink to as few as eight.
body: Essex's Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner Roger Hirst has come out strongly against reported plans to merge police forces, which could see Essex Police lose its standalone status and become part of a larger regional force. The proposals would change how policing is organised for the county's roughly 1.9 million residents.

A review for the Government led by former Metropolitan Police Commissioner Bernard Hogan-Howe is reported to consider cutting England's 39 forces to as few as nine regional forces, plus one for Wales, sitting above more than 150 local policing units. Met Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley used a speech in Manchester on Friday to argue that the 43 forces in England and Wales should become eight to ten, under a new National Police Service, warning that policing faces decline without reform. Mr Hirst said most people at three public meetings he chaired opposed the idea, and a summer survey by his office found 69% of respondents against regional mergers.

The Hogan-Howe review has been sent to the Home Secretary but not published; The Guardian reports it is due out before Christmas, with a white paper in the new year, and that police and crime commissioners would be abolished under the Government's plans. Mr Hirst argues policing should stay locally led and says Essex should not pay the price for problems at the much larger Met, and he wants a fairer funding formula instead. Speaking to the BBC on Saturday, Mr Hirst called the plan not fit for purpose and said there was no evidence that so-called mega forces perform better; the idea has been on pause since Andy Burnham became prime minister in July.

body: A renewable energy company has begun the national planning process for a solar and energy storage park of up to 1 gigawatt on the Dengie Peninsula. The Dengie Peninsula Energy Park would sit on land near Bradwell-on-Sea, Dengie and Burnham-on-Crouch, and its developer Low Carbon says it could power around 250,000 homes.

Because of its size the scheme is a Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project, so it would be examined by the Planning Inspectorate and decided by the Secretary of State rather than Maldon District Council. Low Carbon has asked the Inspectorate to agree which environmental issues must be studied, and the council has been asked for its views. Issues that may be assessed include landscape and views, wildlife, loss of farmland, construction traffic, grid connections, noise, effects on aircraft and glare from panels.

The council must send its comments by 24 November 2026 and is working with Essex County Council on a joint approach. Council leader Simon Morgan said the council would still represent local communities and advise on local impacts. The developer plans a wider public consultation in early 2027 before submitting a formal application.

The plan has been published because the Government formally directed the council to do so, after it signalled it would strip out housing sites and delay this stage.

Housing and Planning Minister Matthew Pennycook wrote to council leader Daniel Cowan on 23 October ordering publication by 6 November, submission for examination by 31 March 2027 and monthly progress reports, Local Government Lawyer reported. The minister pointed to a local plan that is 19 years old and a Housing Delivery Test score that fell to 20% in 2025. Cabinet agreed unanimously on 5 November to publish the draft, and planning portfolio holder Kevin Robinson said: "We have been told quite clearly to publish this plan by the Government".

The Regulation 19 consultation runs from 6 November to 21 December, with documents on the council's Local Plan website and in libraries and the Civic Centre. Comments should address whether the plan is legally compliant and sound. All responses then go to a Planning Inspector for independent examination, and full council will look at the final plan in early 2027.

body: Road closures for Remembrance Sunday parades will disrupt bus services across Essex on Sunday 8 November, with First Essex listing changes in 16 towns and villages from Chelmsford and Colchester to Leigh-on-Sea and Great Dunmow. Most closures fall between mid-morning and lunchtime around the 11am two-minute silence, so anyone travelling on Sunday morning should check their route before setting out. In Chelmsford the service begins at 10.55am at the war memorial in Duke Street, led by the Dean of Chelmsford, while in Southend the parade assembles at Prittlewell Square at 10.15am and moves along Clifftown Parade to the Cenotaph for an 11am service.

In Chelmsford, city centre roads close from 10am to 12.30pm and the bus station cannot be used, so passengers are asked to board at Coval Lane, the Retail Market or Parkway instead. In Colchester, Head Street and High Street close from 8am to 1.30pm, affecting routes including the 51 to 57, 68, 75, 87 and X20. Closures also hit Brentwood High Street from 10.15am to 11.45am, Rayleigh High Street from 9.30am, Wickford's Runwell Road from 10am to 1pm, and the high streets in Maldon, Burnham-on-Crouch and Great Dunmow during the morning.

Afternoon parades bring later closures, with Halstead High Street shut from 2pm to 3pm, Witham's Newland Street from 2.30pm to 3.45pm and Leigh Broadway from 2pm to 5pm. In Saffron Walden, the town council says London Road, High Street, King Street, Market Place and Market Hill close from 9.45am to 12.30pm, with no parking in the affected spots from 5am. First Essex says drivers may also pause for the two-minute silence at 11am where it is safe to do so. Ahead of the services, Essex County Council placed poppy emblems on carriageways at 12 locations, near war memorials where possible, and Thurrock Council teams tidied and repainted memorials in Tilbury, Grays, Aveley, Purfleet and East Tilbury.

body: Essex Police says its roads policing officers arrested 1,960 people on suspicion of drug-driving between 1 January and 31 October 2026, more than twice the number held on suspicion of drink-driving. The figures, released on Saturday, show impaired driving remains one of the biggest pressures on the county's roads as the festive season approaches.

Over the same ten months officers made 886 arrests on suspicion of drink-driving, 313 arrests for failing to provide a breath test and 515 for other drink or drug related road offences, including driving while unfit. Adam Pipe, the force's head of roads policing, said drug-driving arrests were now more than twice drink-driving arrests and warned that any impaired driver could cause a collision that changes or ends a life.

The force is now preparing its annual Christmas campaign warning drivers about getting behind the wheel after alcohol or drugs. Police say patrols will continue alongside intelligence-led operations, roadside drug testing and dedicated roads policing teams targeting repeat and high-risk offenders.

stories.headline: Thurrock's baby death rate is 37% above the national average, new health strategy warns
stories.summary: A draft Health and Wellbeing Strategy for 2027 to 2030 puts pregnancy and the early years at the centre of plans to give Thurrock babies a healthier start.
body: Thurrock records 6.2 infant deaths for every 1,000 live births, against a national average of 3.9, according to the council's proposed Health and Wellbeing Strategy for 2027 to 2030. The figures mean the borough's infant mortality rate is 37% higher than the England average, and the strategy sets out how the council and NHS plan to respond.

Priorities include cutting smoking and obesity in pregnancy, raising breastfeeding rates and improving childhood vaccination uptake, with families offered support earlier. Cllr Rob Willoughby, cabinet member for adults, health and housing, said the causes of the higher rate are complex and that the council will work with health partners so expectant and new parents get the help they need. The report also notes adult life expectancy in Thurrock is the lowest in mid and south Essex.

Councillors on the Adult and Health Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee are due to consider the strategy on Thursday 12 November. The same document cites the 2025 Thurrock Residents Survey, in which 49% of respondents said they worried about their wellbeing after dark, and community safety is one of its four priorities alongside childhood, healthy lifestyles and ageing. The council says a phased delivery plan drawn up with partners, including Essex Police and Essex Fire, will set out specific actions once the strategy is approved.

stories.headline: Basildon councillors refuse 910-home Foots Farm scheme near Billericay's Sun Corner
stories.summary: The planning committee turned down the green belt application off Southend Road, but the developers' appeal is already heading to a public inquiry next May.
body: Basildon Council's planning committee has refused outline plans for 910 homes at Foots Farm, off Southend Road on the edge of Billericay. Campaigners had fought the scheme over its impact on the green belt and on traffic at Sun Corner, the junction at the southern end of the High Street.

The Billericay Action Group says the committee refused the application on 3 November. The developers, Obsidian Strategic, Brentwood Roman Catholic Diocesan Trustee and H.R. Philpot & Son Barleylands, had already appealed to the Planning Inspectorate because the council took too long to decide, Greatest Hits Radio reported in September. They argue the land should count as grey belt, while the action group says Southend Road feeds straight into a junction that is already over capacity.

The appeal is due to go to a public inquiry starting on 11 May 2027, where a planning inspector will make the final decision. Council vice chairman of planning Sam Journet said in September he was extremely unhappy that missed deadlines had taken the decision away from elected councillors.

stories.headline: More than 50,000 still waiting at Southend Hospital as trust backlog falls by 14,000
stories.summary: Hospital chief executive Fiona Ryan told councillors there is still a long way to go, although waiting lists across the Mid and South Essex trust are starting to come down.
body: More than 50,000 patients are still waiting for an appointment or treatment at Southend University Hospital, councillors have been told, even though the backlog across the Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust has fallen by about 14,000 over the past year. The trust also runs Basildon and Broomfield hospitals, so the figures matter to patients across south and mid Essex.

Chief executive Fiona Ryan told Southend-on-Sea City Council's health scrutiny committee on Tuesday that the list was starting to fall but there was "a long way to go". About 9,000 patients join the list each month, and Southend accounted for almost a third of the trust's 165,227 backlog in August. Reform UK councillor John Corrigan suggested some patients referred to Cora Health had simply been moved onto another list; the trust said some care, such as physiotherapy, is better delivered in the community, and accepted Cora has its own waiting list.

The hospital credits extra theatre slots, regular checks on whether patients still need treatment and more use of technology for the progress. It is also expanding patient-initiated follow-ups, which let some patients ask for an appointment when they need one instead of attending on a fixed schedule. The BBC noted the trust was previously ranked worst in England for starting cancer treatment within 62 days.

stories.headline: Labour calls for Reform to expel Great Notley county councillor over deleted social media post
stories.summary: Carl Johnson, who represents Three Fields and Great Notley on Essex County Council, says he was exercising free speech after Labour branded his post about the Home Secretary and London mayor racist.
body: A Reform UK county councillor from the Braintree district is at the centre of a row over a social media post that Labour says was racist. Carl Johnson represents the Three Fields and Great Notley division on Essex County Council, which Reform runs.

The post, shared on Wednesday and later removed, showed Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood next to London mayor Sadiq Khan with a caption claiming the country had been infiltrated, alongside a line saying no foreigner should stand for political office. Both were born in the UK. Labour county councillor Lee Scordis called the post xenophobic and urged Reform to expel him, while Mr Johnson told the Local Democracy Reporting Service that open debate should not be shut down because others disagree.

A Reform spokesperson said Councillor Johnson is entitled to his own personal views, and Braintree Conservatives said they strongly oppose the remarks. Essex County Council said it was aware of the post but would not say whether it had received a complaint.

stories.headline: Brentwood Centre revamp cost rises to £29m as planned spa is dropped
stories.summary: Councillors will consider a final business case on 12 November, with every recommendation depending on Full Council finding an extra £3.82m.
body: The cost of redeveloping the Brentwood Centre has risen to up to £29.02m, about £4m more than the £25m approved in September, and the planned spa has been cut from the scheme. The leisure centre is one of the borough's biggest public investments, so the extra money will be closely watched by residents.

Brentwood Borough Council's share would rise from £23m to £26.82m, with a £2.2m Football Foundation grant covering pitches and related facilities. Building tenders came in over budget, so the design was scaled back: the spa space becomes a health hub with dry changing rooms, the first-floor extension is now single-storey and the foyer has been redesigned to include football changing rooms. Officers describe the scheme as financially supportable but a significant commitment with material delivery risks.

The Assets and Strategy Committee will consider the final business case on Thursday 12 November, and every recommendation depends on Full Council agreeing the extra £3.82m. Start and completion dates are still to be confirmed; the council says the centre will stay open as far as possible, but tenants leasing space must move out before building begins.

stories.headline: South Basildon MP James McMurdock raises alarm over how few refused asylum claims end in returns
stories.summary: Home Office figures show only around one in ten asylum claims refused from 2025 has so far led to a recorded return, and the MP for South Basildon and East Thurrock wants the Government to publish clearer data.
body: James McMurdock, MP for South Basildon and East Thurrock, has raised concerns about the small share of refused asylum claims that lead to a recorded return, as well as long appeal waits and a growing backlog. He said a refusal should not become the start of years of delay and uncertainty, and called the backlog unacceptable.

Home Office figures reported alongside his comments show about 3,300 returns had been recorded by July 2026 for claims made in 2025, against about 34,300 claims whose latest outcome was refusal, roughly 10%. The share of refused claims ending in a recorded return fell from 55% in 2022 to 13% in 2024. At the end of June 2026 about 90,000 asylum appeals were outstanding, with an average wait of around 72 weeks, and 32,400 applications were awaiting an initial decision.

Mr McMurdock is urging the Government to provide clear reporting on how many refused claimants are ultimately returned. The figures do not necessarily mean every other refused claimant remains in the UK: some people leave before a decision, some are removed for other reasons and some refusals are still under appeal.

stories.headline: Parking at Princess Alexandra Hospital in Harlow to cost more from 17 November
stories.summary: The trust says the rise is a small inflation-linked increase, with the first 20 minutes staying free and existing exemptions kept.
body: Patients and visitors parking at Princess Alexandra Hospital in Harlow will pay slightly more from Tuesday 17 November, the hospital trust has announced. The trust describes the change as a small inflationary increase designed to keep charges in step with the cost of running and maintaining its car parks.

The rise is based on the April 2026 Consumer Prices Index rate of 2.6%, rounded to the nearest 10p. A stay of up to one hour goes from £3.50 to £3.60, up to two hours from £5 to £5.20, and 12 to 24 hours from £15 to £15.40. Chief People Officer Catrin Asbrey said the trust had kept the increase as small as possible.

The first 20 minutes remain free, and free parking continues for Blue Badge holders, parents and guardians staying overnight with young patients, frequent outpatient attendees and others with particular needs. The trust says regular small rises avoid a bigger jump later, following a 2025 review that brought in shorter tariff bands.

stories.summary: Three councils have opened a single online hub for the planned new town east of Colchester, with a decision on its planning application expected in summer 2027.
body: Colchester City Council, Tendring District Council and Essex County Council have launched a new website for the Tendring Colchester Borders Garden Community. The site brings the project's plans, progress, documents and ways to get involved into one place for residents and businesses.

Master developer Latimer by Clarion Housing has submitted a hybrid planning application for 7,750 homes in three neighbourhoods between Colchester and Tendring, with 30% affordable housing, schools, jobs space and community facilities. The councils say 51% of the site would be open space, including a new Salary Brook Country Park. The first phase of the A1331 link road has opened and will eventually connect to the A120.

No decision has yet been made: the application is expected to go before the garden community's joint committee in summer 2027. Colchester council leader Paul Dundas said the website gives everyone a simple way to see how the community is taking shape.

stories.headline: Transport Secretary tours Stansted as airport pushes on with plan for 51 million passengers
stories.summary: Heidi Alexander saw the new skylink walkways, the enlarged security hall and the airport's solar farm during a visit to London Stansted.
body: Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander has visited London Stansted to see progress on its five-year transformation programme, as the airport works towards handling 51 million passengers a year over the next two decades without a new runway. Stansted is Essex's biggest single employer site and carried more than 30 million passengers in 2025, with record monthly numbers so far in 2026.

Capital delivery programme director Rob Stewart briefed her on the skylink walkways that will link the terminal directly to the satellite buildings, allowing the track transit people mover to be taken out of service and freeing space for a three-bay, 16,500 square metre terminal extension. She also toured the enlarged security hall and the airfield, and saw the on-site solar farm that opened in September. Ms Alexander said the government backs airport growth that balances the economy with climate, noise and air quality duties, and praised the solar farm.

Managing director Gareth Powell said the visit showed the momentum behind the airport's plans. Stansted says it contributes £11.3 billion a year to the economy, according to York Aviation, and is aiming for net zero in its direct operations by 2038 at the latest. No completion date was given for the walkways or later phases.

stories.headline: Peter Swift wins World Sausage Throwing Championship on Harwich Green for third year running
stories.summary: The 29-year-old hurled an out-of-date banger 148.5ft to keep his title at the quirky contest run by Tendring Camra, while a Great Bromley butcher took the Champion Sausage of Tendring prize.
body: Peter Swift has won the World Sausage Throwing Championship on Harwich Green for the third year in a row, BBC News reported. The 29-year-old's winning throw measured 148.5ft (45.26m), though the competition record of 171ft (52.12m), set by Todd Rothwell in 2019, still stands.

The event has been run since 2011 by the Tendring branch of the Campaign for Real Ale, and organiser Richard Oxborrow said it began in a pub as a quirky way to promote the local beer festival. Each competitor has two throws using out-of-date sausages. Swift's advice was to be gentle with the sausage, because crumpling it into a ball makes it burst, and he praised Harwich's community spirit and its pubs.

Among this year's field was Mark Rye, 47, from Cardiff, who was making his 70th world championship entry and persuaded organisers to adopt the World Sausage Throwing Championship name. Alongside the throwing, nine butchers competed for Champion Sausage of Tendring, which went to Becky's Butchers in Great Bromley for a sweet chilli sausage.

stories.headline: E-bike pods at Harwich station and on the harbour ferry aim to keep coastal visitors moving
stories.summary: Greater Anglia and Freeport East have launched the Harwich Haven Eezybike Connect network, with five pods at stations and on the Harwich Harbour Ferry.
body: Rail and ferry passengers around Harwich can now pick up an electric bike for the last leg of their journey after Greater Anglia launched a new e-bike network on the Essex and Suffolk coast. The scheme, called Harwich Haven Eezybike Connect, puts five e-bike pods at railway stations, including Harwich Town, and on the Harwich Harbour Ferry.

The network was developed by Freeport East, the area's Industrial Strategy Zone, and received a £25,600 grant from Greater Anglia's Customer and Community Improvement Fund, which is backing 33 projects this year. Pod locations were chosen to line up with local hotels and Shotley Marina, with the aim of encouraging visitors to stay longer. Greater Anglia's partnerships manager Scott Dolling said the project makes it easier for customers to carry on their journeys beyond the railway.

Felixstowe station across the estuary in Suffolk is also part of the network. Greater Anglia says the bikes offer a low-carbon way to explore lesser-known corners of the harbour area, and the full list of pods and hire details is published by the operator.

stories.headline: Water workers find a carpet python hissing in a Vange meter chamber during leak repair
stories.summary: The cold and injured snake, probably someone's pet, is being cared for by South Essex Wildlife Hospital, which will rehome it if no owner comes forward.
body: An Essex and Suffolk Water crew fixing a leak in Vange, Basildon, stopped work after hearing hissing from a meter chamber and found a carpet python inside. The non-venomous snake, native to Australia and New Guinea, measured three to four feet and is thought to have been a pet.

The crew called South Essex Wildlife Hospital, whose volunteers from Orsett collected the snake and confirmed the species. It was dehydrated, cold and injured, and founder Sue Schwar said it was not very happy when it arrived. The water company said its engineers had come across plenty in their work, but a python was a first.

How the python ended up underground is not known, and the hospital suggested it may have escaped down a toilet or been dumped. It is now being treated, and the hospital says it will look for a new home for the snake if its owner does not come forward.

stories.headline: Wildlife groups take 55,000-name petition to Google over data centre plan for Purfleet's old Arena Essex site
stories.summary: Buglife and Essex Wildlife Trust say the scheme would wipe out most of a protected wildlife site, while Google says it will regenerate the land and deliver a 10% biodiversity gain.
body: Campaigners have taken a petition with nearly 55,000 names to Google's London headquarters, urging the company to drop plans for a data centre on the former Arena Essex Raceway near Purfleet. The 52-hectare site was designated a Local Wildlife Site in 2006, and conservationists say it supports hundreds of species including rare bees, butterflies and nightingales.

Google's proposal is for up to four data centre buildings totalling 130,500 square metres, plus a separate office building. Buglife programmes manager Jamie Robins said it was the wrong place for a data centre, and Emily Buttress of Essex Wildlife Trust warned the loss would further break up the local ecological network. The groups say more than 80 per cent of the site's protected habitats would be lost, and they claim staff at Google's offices refused to accept the petition, which the company neither confirmed nor denied.

Google says data centres are vital to UK digital services and that its plans would bring investment and jobs to Thurrock. It says it is working with Natural England to deliver a 10% biodiversity net gain and that a large part of the site would remain as public open space and retained habitat. Campaigners want the land opened as green space, alongside a return for Thurrock Hammers Speedway.

features.summary: A Colchester restaurant took both the county and national chef titles, and Kelvedon Spice was named Essex Restaurant of the Year.
body: Essex restaurants and takeaways had a strong night at the 2026 Asian Restaurant and Takeaway Awards, the ceremony often called the Curry Oscars. Essex Life reports that county venues won regional titles and two of the night's national prizes.

Kusturi Indian Restaurant in Colchester was named both Essex Chef of the Year and National Chef of the Year, while Kelvedon Spice won Essex Restaurant of the Year. Kaani Kaana in Upminster took Essex Takeaway of the Year and the national takeaway title. Moonlight Tandoori in Harlow, Crown of India in Loughton and Pink Chilliz on Canvey were among the other Essex finalists.

The awards were presented on October 12 at the London Hilton on Park Lane, hosted by news presenter Samantha Simmonds and comedian Paul Sinha. ARTA founder and chief executive Mohammed Munim congratulated all the winners and finalists.

features.headline: From hedgerow to cheeseboard: what to eat in Essex this autumn
features.summary: Essex Life asks a forager and an award-winning cheesemaker what the county's larder has to offer as the nights draw in.
body: Apples, oysters, game, honey and cheese all hit their stride in autumn, and Essex Life has gone looking for the best of the county's seasonal larder, with a few foraged surprises along the way.

At The Foraging Chef, the season is treated as an adventure: wild mushrooms, and hedgerow fruits such as rosehips, crab apples and sloes, are at their peak. Muntjac also feature, with the case made that eating the deer puts a plentiful local food to use while helping to keep numbers in check.

Bradfields Farm Dairy talks through the cheeses locals keep coming back for, including its soft Beam and an Essex herb cheese. For a warm autumn day it suggests its Bourne Brook spread over a barbecue skewer with aubergines and marmande tomatoes from Sarah Green Organics and a drizzle of Essex rapeseed oil.

features.headline: An eight-mile ramble along the Mardyke, one of Essex's least-known rivers
features.summary: A countryside circuit from South Ockendon's round-tower church follows the Mardyke Way past fields, solar farms and wildlife.
body: Essex Life's latest walk starts at St Nicholas of Myra Church on The Green in South Ockendon and loops for about eight miles along the Mardyke Way. The Mardyke, sometimes written Mar Dyke, is a small, overgrown river in a wide, flat valley crossed by the M25 and A13 near junction 30.

South Ockendon has been a village since at least Saxon times, with signs of Roman settlement near South Ockendon Hall. Its church keeps fine Norman details and is one of only six in Essex with a round tower. The route heads out past the Royal Oak pub and the hall before crossing the river by a metal footbridge.
Ockendon station is about 500 metres from the start along West Road. Davy Down Riverside Park, just west of the route, has parking and toilets.

The ground floor has a living room, sitting room, separate dining room, a study and a piano room, built around a large kitchen and diner that opens on to the garden. Four bedrooms are on the first floor, many with en suites and walk-in wardrobes, and two more sit on the second floor with a family bathroom.

body: Frinton-based painter Simon Carter has turned Firstsite in Colchester into a walk-through painting for From the Landscape, the largest exhibition of his career.

The show blends painting, architecture and sound. Carter has built monolithic walls modelled on the groynes that protect the Essex shoreline, and added a soundscape made from his own recordings of the coast. Firstsite director Sally Shaw says he has been quietly mapping the Essex landscape for more than forty years.
The exhibition is supported by the Firstsite Collectors' Group and Trevor Fenwick, and is listed to run until 17 January 2027.

councilwatch.headline: Tendring budgets for life beyond 2028 as the government pauses the council shake-up
councilwatch.summary: With Whitehall reviewing its plan to replace Essex's councils, Tendring's cabinet has agreed to plan four years ahead, and backed money for toilets, playgrounds and housing staff.
body: Tendring District Council's cabinet has agreed to refresh the council's financial forecast over four years, to allow for the possibility that the council still exists after April 2028. That date had been the proposed start for a new unitary council under the government's original timetable for Greater Essex, but on 7 September 2026 the government announced it would pause and review its local government reorganisation programme.

The report to cabinet on 23 October said the pause had brought a significant level of uncertainty for the councils affected, though Tendring's two-year financial plan still left it in a positive position. If reorganisation goes ahead, even later than planned, the forecast can be switched back to the council's earlier approach of preparing for a handover to the new authority.

Cabinet also approved changes to this year's budget, including £540,000 for housing capacity and restructuring, £100,000 to invest in public toilets and £400,000 for project delivery capacity, and accepted £270,000 from the government's Playground Fund. The report said the general fund was £3.669m underspent against its profiled budget at the end of July, largely because of the timing of spending.
points: Forecast to be refreshed over four years in case the council continues beyond April 2028
Government paused its reorganisation programme on 7 September 2026
£270,000 Playground Fund grant accepted and £100,000 set aside for public toilets
General fund £3.669m underspent at the end of July, mostly down to timing

councilwatch.headline: Thurrock's special needs funding gap keeps growing as Treetops School plans 110 more places
councilwatch.summary: Children's services are on course to underspend by about £0.5m, but the grant that pays for special educational needs is heading deeper into deficit, councillors heard.
body: Thurrock Council's children's services are forecast to underspend by about £0.5 million this year, councillors on the Children's Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee heard on 22 October. Officers said the underspend came largely from making the most of grants and from staff vacancies, which offset rising demand, and that all planned savings had been achieved.

The committee was also told about pressure on the high needs block of the Dedicated Schools Grant, which pays for special educational needs provision. Officers said forecasts showed a growing deficit despite investment in local specialist places, and that national funding arrangements and reform proposals would be critical to its long-term sustainability, with government support expected to cover a substantial part of the deficit.

Officers confirmed that 110 additional places were planned at Treetops School through a phased expansion, which would add local specialist capacity and reduce reliance on placements outside the borough. They said feedback from the Department for Education on the council's submission had been positive, focusing on extra detail and measurable outcomes rather than finances. The committee noted the forecast.
points: Children's services forecast to underspend by about £0.5m
High needs deficit growing despite investment in local places
110 more places planned at Treetops School in a phased expansion
Government support expected to cover a substantial part of the deficit

councilwatch.headline: Thurrock picked as one of seven national pilots helping children stay with their wider family
councilwatch.summary: The Kinship Zones pilot will give practical, emotional and financial support to relatives raising children, as Thurrock reshapes its children's social care.
body: Thurrock has been selected as one of seven national Kinship Zones pilot authorities, councillors heard at the Children's Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee on 22 October. The pilot aims to help children stay safely within their wider family networks, with practical, emotional and financial support for kinship carers and fewer care proceedings.

It is part of the council's Families First Partnership programme, which aims to step in earlier and support whole families. Officers said ten Family Help Teams had been set up and a single assessment and planning framework introduced, and that work was under way on a Multi-Agency Child Protection Team bringing together professionals from partner organisations.

The committee also heard that 75% of initial health assessments for children entering care were now completed within the statutory 20 days, up from 36% previously. Officers credited closer joint working, more paediatric capacity and better oversight, and said a formal review of the new nurse-led and paediatrician model would take place in December 2026.
points: One of seven national Kinship Zones pilot authorities
Ten Family Help Teams now in place
75% of health checks for children entering care now on time, up from 36%
Review of the new health assessment model due in December

councilwatch.headline: Southend's fraud investigators have brought in more than £800,000 for the council this year
councilwatch.summary: School admissions fraud and Blue Badge misuse were among the areas councillors raised as the council's counter fraud team reported on its work.
body: Southend-on-Sea City Council's Counter Fraud and Investigation Team has generated benefits of more than £800,000 for the council so far this financial year, the Audit and Governance Committee heard on 19 October.

Councillors discussed recent work on school admissions fraud. Officers said referrals came from school admissions officers, members of the public and the team's own proactive investigations, and that growing public awareness had led to more referrals. Members also asked about Blue Badge enforcement and future investigation exercises.

The committee heard that a new fraud investigator had been recruited and that a number of investigations involving council employees were continuing. Officers said details could not be disclosed for confidentiality reasons, but that criminal prosecutions continued to be pursued where appropriate. The committee noted the report.
points: Benefits of more than £800,000 so far this financial year
More school admissions fraud referrals as awareness grows
Blue Badge enforcement raised by councillors
New fraud investigator recruited
